clue.text: Somewhere on vacation away?

indicators.note: a word on vacation has been emptied out, leaving only its outside letters standing

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
aside means away, to one side

explanation.surface: A riddle asking where you might be when you are away on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read as a riddle it defines the answer, and every word also feeds the wordplay, which makes it an &lit.
explanation.definitionFit: A coastal resort is the classic British holiday destination, the place people go when they are off work.

clue.text: Time spent drinking nip of Scotch, what about second?

indicators.note: a nip is a small sip, so only a tiny first taste of the word is taken
about means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
eh? is a way of saying what? when you have not heard
S is the standard abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: Someone at a bar takes a nip of whisky and asks what happened to the second one.
explanation.definitionFit: A sesh is informal slang for a session, especially a long stretch of heavy drinking with friends.

clue.text: Recklessly leave in car, drunk

indicators.note: someone drunk is all over the place, so these letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning about someone who drunkenly abandons a car and its occupants.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a French phrase found in Chambers, meaning in a cavalier, offhand manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting in a cavalier way means behaving with haughty disregard for consequences, which is careless and rash conduct.

clue.text: Bypass increases twofold after first curve

indicators.note: the letter following the opening one is swapped for a Roman numeral worth double its value

blocks.note: to bypass something is to go round it

explanation.surface: A road bypass carrying twice the traffic once the first bend is reached.
explanation.walkthrough: V is the Roman numeral five and X is ten, so V doubled becomes X; the letter changed is the one right after the first.
explanation.definitionFit: An axoid is a technical term for a ruled surface or curve traced out by a moving axis in kinematics.

clue.text: Perhaps whiskey from fair is hooch?

indicators.note: from says the letters are drawn out of the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A drinker wonders whether whiskey from a fair is really bootleg liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling whiskey with an E is the usual Irish and American one; Scotch is whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Whiskey from Ireland is one example of the nationality adjective, so 'perhaps' signals a definition by example.

clue.text: Come back to work in the morning fit to return after party

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so this word is read backwards

blocks.note: a do is a party
AM marks hours before noon
fit as in capable

explanation.surface: Someone recovering after a party wonders if they are fit enough to go back to the office in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase recalls the soprano Nellie Melba, famous for her many farewell concerts followed by yet more comebacks.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to make repeated returns from retirement, like the singer who kept giving final performances.

clue.text: Contributions to NI? Irishman’s about to invest money

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word is read from end to start
investing something means wrapping it up inside, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: Pat is a stock Irish name, with the possessive S
M is a standard abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: An Irishman puts money into Northern Ireland as his contribution.
explanation.walkthrough: NI looks like Northern Ireland beside the Irishman, but it is National Insurance, the British social security payment once recorded by sticking stamps on a card.
explanation.definitionFit: National Insurance contributions were once paid by buying stamps fixed to a weekly card, so the word stood for the payment itself.

clue.text: Strong suggestion of stench by dunny?

indicators.note: a mere suggestion is only a hint, so just the opening letter is used

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
an obscure dialect word for a privy or outhouse; dunny is Australian slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A smell drifts from beside an outdoor toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Stout means sturdy, robust and powerful, the sense in stout walls or a stout defence.

clue.text: Superb century after doubling into pocket set back champion

indicators.note: doubling into suggests the pieces fold together side by side, one directly after the other
something set back is pushed the other way, so the pair is read in reverse

blocks.note: a ton is a hundred
a pot is a pocket on a billiard table
CH is the abbreviation for champion

explanation.surface: A batsman's century and a ball into the pocket mark out a champion.
explanation.definitionFit: Something first-rate is of the highest quality, as if marked at the uppermost notch on a scale.

clue.text: Friendly relations a disaster lacking calibre

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so these letters are taken away

blocks.note: a calamity is a disaster
CAL is the abbreviation for calibre

explanation.surface: Diplomatic ties collapse when a nation lacks the calibre to keep them.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is peaceful goodwill between people or nations, the state of being on good terms.

clue.text: Religious festival eg, plugging God year after year

blocks.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild
taken as written
YR is the abbreviation for year
Y is another abbreviation for year

explanation.surface: A holy feast, for instance one promoting God, held year after year.
explanation.walkthrough: Year is abbreviated two different ways here, once as YR and once as Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A panegyry is a rare word for a solemn church celebration or public festal assembly.

clue.text: Dryness in mouth possibly moister on account of ensuing kiss

indicators.note: possibly hints that the letters might be arranged some other way
ensuing means following, so the rearranged letters come after the other piece

blocks.note: X stands for a kiss at the end of a letter
taken as written, to be rearranged
O/A is the abbreviation for on account

explanation.surface: A mouth might feel moister after a kiss, curing its dryness.
explanation.definitionFit: Xerostomia is the medical term for a lack of saliva, from Greek roots meaning dry and mouth.

clue.text: Boisterous social drinking-songs

indicators.note: boisterous suggests rowdy disorder, so the letters are tumbled about

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Rowdy party songs sung over drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: A scolion was a song sung in turn by guests at an ancient Greek banquet; scolia is its plural.

clue.text: American chaps propose marriage alongside home of poet

definitions.note: adjective: relating to the poet Alexander Pope

indicators.note: used as a verb, to chap is to crack open, so one word splits the other apart

blocks.note: from pop the question
A is the abbreviation for American
in means at home

explanation.surface: American men pop the question near the house where a poet lived.
explanation.walkthrough: Chaps looks like a noun meaning men, but it is a verb meaning cracks open.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to or in the style of Alexander Pope, the eighteenth-century English satirical writer.

clue.text: Die with courage? Sadly that’s bitter-sweet

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters come out in a different order

blocks.note: with is a link inside the fodder phrase; the ten letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dying bravely but sadly is a mixed experience.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French for sour-sweet, used in English mainly of sauces.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase describes a sweet and sour flavour, combining tartness and sugar in one dish.

clue.text: Arab chief almost top to bottom in cloths

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
in a down light the top is the first letter, and it is moved to the bottom end

blocks.note: a variant spelling of sheikh

explanation.surface: An Arab leader wears robes from head to foot.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of the chief to get SHAIK, then move its first letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A haik is a large piece of fabric worn wrapped round the head and body in North Africa.

clue.text: Second release, one from The Police in NA

definitions.text: one from The Police in NA

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, as in half a mo
to untie is to set free

explanation.surface: A record label issues a second single by The Police in North America.
explanation.walkthrough: The Police looks like the rock band, but here it is a police force; NA is North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounties are members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the federal force of Canada in North America.

clue.text: Native American having whim about historical part of Kent

indicators.note: having means holding, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: a fad is a passing whim
the lathes were ancient administrative divisions of the English county of Kent

explanation.surface: An indigenous American takes a fancy to the history of an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: Flathead is a name for certain North American peoples, such as the Salish of Montana, once said to shape infants' skulls.

clue.text: US conduct I have reformed in nick repulsed

indicators.note: reformed means made again in a new shape, so these letters are rearranged
in places the rearranged letters inside the other word
repulsed means driven back, so the whole is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to nick is to steal

explanation.surface: A prisoner swears he has reformed his conduct in jail, though his plea is rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: US flags the American spelling without the U.
explanation.definitionFit: Behavior is the American spelling of the word for how a person acts or comports themselves.

clue.text: Bullion bagging lag a rich source of wealth

indicators.note: bagging means capturing in a bag, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: bullion is gold in bars
a lag and a con are both convicts
taken as written

explanation.surface: A convict pockets gold bars.
explanation.definitionFit: Golconda, an Indian city famed for its diamond mines, became a byword for an inexhaustible mine of riches.

clue.text: What’s largely unruly drinking in part of sports ground?

definitions.text: What’s largely unruly drinking in part of sports ground?

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the preceding word's letters are scattered
drinking means taking in, so the shuffled letters swallow another piece

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the outer is the part of a ground outside the enclosure

explanation.surface: Asks what describes mostly rowdy boozing in the stands at a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue serves as definition and wordplay at once. A lager lout is British slang for a young man who drinks beer and turns rowdy.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names drunken hooliganism by beer-swilling youths, a behaviour notorious at British football matches.

clue.text: Drug baron hiding in a cupboard?

indicators.note: something hiding in a place is tucked inside it

blocks.note: Alpha is the radio code word for the letter A
B is the abbreviation for baron
a locker is a small cupboard

explanation.surface: A drug lord hides in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Drug baron reads as one phrase, but drug is the definition and baron gives a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This medicine blocks certain adrenaline receptors, relaxing blood vessels to treat high blood pressure.

clue.text: Fashion victim’s first to be overwhelmed by charge

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word before it
being overwhelmed means being engulfed, so this letter goes inside

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
something in your charge is in your care

explanation.surface: A fashion victim is buried under the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Fashion victim sounds like one phrase; fashion is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To fashion something can mean to shape it from wood or stone, which is to sculpt or cut it.

clue.text: Hard engraving back of exquisite arrangement of stones?

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
ENG is the abbreviation for engraving
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Engraving the reverse of a fine gem setting is difficult.
explanation.definitionFit: A henge is a prehistoric circular monument, such as Stonehenge, often with standing megaliths.

clue.text: Largely hurry to government shelter in Scotland

indicators.note: largely means mostly but not wholly, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: to scoot is to dash off
G is the abbreviation for government

explanation.surface: Someone rushes to the government for refuge in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoog is a Scots dialect word for a place of cover or refuge from the weather.

clue.text: Regularly echo Lorelei to call for attention

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: The siren of the Rhine's voice keeps echoing back, demanding to be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lorelei is the legendary siren of the Rhine, whose calls lured sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooee is a long shrill call first used in the Australian bush to attract someone at a distance.

clue.text: Close to pipeline drilling must come to a standstill

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is used
drilling means boring into, so this letter goes inside the phrase

blocks.note: must means have to
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Drilling near a pipeline must halt.
explanation.definitionFit: To heave to is a nautical term for bringing a ship to a halt with its head to the wind.

clue.text: What’s necessary on opening of claret — a little pop?

definitions.text: What’s necessary on opening of claret — a little pop?

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
a little of the word means just its first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
a necessary, or necessary house, is an old word for a privy; a loo is a toilet
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Asks what is needed to open a bottle of red wine with a gentle pop.
explanation.walkthrough: What's necessary looks like a requirement, but necessary is a noun for a privy. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloop is the hollow sound a cork makes when it is drawn from a bottle.

clue.text: Soft saddle about right for horse

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the letter

blocks.note: a pad is a soft saddle
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A cushioned saddle for a horse, with a note on being correct.
explanation.walkthrough: Soft wants to give P, as in music, but here the soft saddle is one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Prad is old slang for a horse, recorded in Chambers.

clue.text: Offending cutting head off fish

indicators.note: cutting the head off removes the opening letter of the word

blocks.note: a herring is a fish

explanation.surface: A sinner chops the head off a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Erring means doing wrong, straying from what is right, so it fits sinning or transgressing.

clue.text: Scotland’s well-known excursion cancelled?

blocks.note: no as in none, nothing happening
a tour is an excursion

explanation.surface: A famous Scottish trip is called off.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads excursion cancelled as no tour.
explanation.definitionFit: Notour is an old Scots legal term meaning notorious, widely known or publicly recognised.

clue.text: Italian official lived years around Vatican City with own goal to worship

indicators.note: around here means turned about, so these letters are read backwards

blocks.note: VA abbreviates Latin vixit annos, he lived so many years, seen on tombstones
V is the international code for Vatican City
OG is the abbreviation for own goal
to adore is to worship

explanation.surface: An Italian official's career summed up by years near the Vatican and a footballing blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: An avvogadore was a state prosecutor or public advocate in the Venetian republic.

clue.text: Poet’s dismal ballad reread in part

indicators.note: in part says only a portion of the words is used, a run of letters within them

blocks.note: the letters run across the word boundary

explanation.surface: A gloomy ballad is read again.
explanation.walkthrough: Poet's flags a word used by Spenser rather than in everyday English.
explanation.definitionFit: Drere is a Spenserian spelling of drear, the archaic form meaning gloomy and cheerless.

clue.text: Witch’s offspring brewing snake’s and dog’s tails with heads

indicators.note: the tail of a word is its last letter
brewing means stewing together, so the letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: the last letter of the word before the apostrophe
the last letter of the word before the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A witch stirring a potion of snake and dog parts in her cauldron.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Tempest, Prospero calls Caliban, son of the witch Sycorax, by this insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Hag-seed is Shakespeare's term for the child of a hag, meaning a witch's brood.
